title: Bounded operating envelope for photophoretic / thermal-transpiration lift
question: What do peer-reviewed experiments and models actually establish about photophoretic (radiometric / thermal-transpiration) levitation at low pressure - achievable lift or payload per unit area, the pressure and Knudsen-number regime, heat-balance and material limits, and scaling - and where precisely is the boundary between measured centimetre-scale demonstrations and modelled payload, altitude or Mars extrapolations?
why_now: Products has been assigned the first end-to-end Product-Potential pilot with a mandatory falsification gate: hold or reject if the Engineering baseline shows no useful payload/force margin inside a realistically manufacturable material and thermal envelope. That gate cannot be applied while 'centimeter-scale experimental demonstrations' and 'modelled payload/scaling claims and Mars extrapolation' remain separated only by assertion; a sourced envelope is needed to judge whether any sensing payload is physically available.
real_world_anchor: Photophoresis / radiometric force and thermal transpiration at low pressure: peer-reviewed levitation experiments, measured lift or payload capacity versus pressure, and the modelling assumptions used to extrapolate to payload scale or Mars conditions.
